chapter_theme: Neelakesi ends the debate with the Vaisheshika teacher Ulokan: she holds quality and action to be both one with and other than their bearer, argues that karma, merit and guilt could not bind or be shed if they were separate from the soul, takes apart generality, particularity and inherence, wins him over by the method of standpoints, and leaves him to worship at the Lord's shrine.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Vaisheshika teacher of Kanada's school whom Neelakesi debates in this sarukkam

804.reading: Neelakesi states her own position: the saying that the qualities are the qualified thing also holds, without contradiction the qualities are found in the substance, and the being and not-being of their twoness (one and different) together make a doctrine worth revering.
804.nuance: Line 3's இருமைய தின்மை உண்மையும் is the Jain both-ways answer: the quality is one with and other than its bearer. Against the Buddhist in 393 she defended the bearer; here, against a school that makes quality a separate category, she defends the oneness.

claims.claim: qualities are both one with and different from the substance that bears them

805.reading: Neelakesi says the many uses things have come through their qualities, by knowing and by closeness, as clay and gold serve through the qualities that stand in them; nothing works except through that intimate union.
805.nuance: Line 2's செண்பினான் is obscure; the clay and gold of line 3 are the stock examples of a substance that keeps its kind through changing forms.

claims.claim: a thing serves any use only through the qualities joined in it

806.reading: Neelakesi argues that the goodness that fetches a price, the evil that is loathed, and the guilt of killing and theft stay as qualities in the person who bears them, a settled oneness; call them separate and nothing would follow.
806.nuance: The metaphysical point is pressed through ethics: if virtue and the guilt of killing and stealing were not the doer's own qualities, praise and blame could not reach the doer.

claims.claim: virtue and the guilt of killing and theft belong to the doer as his own qualities
qualities are separate from the substance that bears them

807.reading: Neelakesi says that falling into good deeds and bad, and reaping fruits as many deeds ripen, belong to the soul as its qualities; if those qualities were ever separate from it, the round of births and release would be empty words.
807.nuance: The stake of the whole quality debate is named here: if karma's fruits do not inhere in the soul, nothing is bound and nothing is freed. Both good and bad deeds (நல்வினை, தீவினை) are counted as binding.

claims.claim: good and bad deeds and their ripened fruits are qualities of the soul itself
if deeds were separate from the soul, rebirth and release would be meaningless

808.reading: Neelakesi argues that the dancer's dancing and the running horse's running belong to the one combined thing, so action too must be granted to be one with its bearer.
808.nuance: This answers the Vaisheshika category of action (கருமம், தொழில்) as she answered quality: the dance is not a thing that could be found apart from the dancer.

claims.claim: action is one with the substance that acts
action is a category separate from substance

809.reading: Neelakesi says the dancers' dancing, the horse's running, recitation of scripture and every other act that has stopped are not lost; they persist in their bearer and come forth again when called for.
809.nuance: Action is treated as a capacity that stays latent in the substance, not as an event that perishes when it ceases; this is how she can call it one with its bearer.

claims.claim: an action that has ceased persists as a capacity in its bearer and returns when needed

810.reading: Neelakesi tells Ulokan that he has not grasped how qualities and actions, distinct yet not at odds, gather, pass away and come to reside together in the substance, and that the fault lies with him.
810.nuance: Line 2 reads குழுமிக கெட்டன without the doubled consonant, and line 4's அதுவும் நின்னுடையதே பிற is hard to construe; the reading follows the drift of the argument.

811.reading: Turning to generality, Neelakesi argues that if the universal stands joined to every thing it would be a oneness making all things one, and if it does not join them, saying that it went into them is empty.
811.nuance: Line 1 is printed பாதுவெலா, plainly for பொதுவெலா (the universal, பொது); line 4's செதுவலாம் is obscure. The dilemma itself (all one, or not joined at all) is clear.

claims.claim: a single generality resides in every thing of its kind

812.reading: Neelakesi presses further: since he says the universal has entered endless things, it must be scattered into many, shrinking, joining and staying, and going without any use; what then has it become?

claims.claim: one generality cannot be present whole in endless separate things

813.reading: Neelakesi says that what is called the universal is only likeness, so the things called common are simply things that resemble one another; and she asks why, if he counts such a thing again among six categories, he does not add this one and make seven.
813.nuance: போலி (line 1) gives the Jain account of the universal as similarity among things, not a separate entity. The jibe about counting seven turns on the Vaisheshika list of six categories (ஆறு, line 3).

claims.claim: what is called the universal is only the likeness of things to one another
the categories are six

814.reading: Neelakesi says that particularity, examined, is just the quality that stands fully in the thing itself, so it too has no being of its own, and she will throw out his count of categories.
814.nuance: Line 4 reads பொருள ளெண்ணலே with a doubled ள.

claims.claim: particularity is a separate category
particularity is only the thing's own quality

815.reading: Neelakesi argues against inherence: if there is no joining except by a joiner, then the inherence that goes to join must itself be joined by another, and so on; she asks whether he piles up many useless things as if reciting verses.
815.nuance: The regress is clear in lines 1-2; line 4's முனிவு போக்கிதோ is hard to construe, and the sense of பாட்டினால் (line 3) is a guess.

claims.claim: quality and substance are joined by a separate relation of inherence
a relation that joins things must itself be joined, so inherence leads to endless regress

816.reading: Neelakesi dares Ulokan to make the heron take blackness and dry ginger take astringency, and so do away with difference once and for all, and laughs that this learned man is to be pitied.
816.nuance: If inherence could join any quality to any substance, nothing would stop black from inhering in the white heron; the absurd test shows a quality belongs to its own bearer by nature.
816.event: Neelakesi challenges Ulokan to join blackness to a heron and laughs at him.

claims.claim: if inherence joined qualities from outside, any quality could be joined to any thing

817.reading: Neelakesi concludes that since things and their natures always arrive together as one, they are one, and since the twoness he needs is not found, there is nothing left for inherence to join.

claims.claim: a thing and its nature always come together as one, leaving nothing for inherence to join

818.reading: An exchange: Ulokan asks why she calls substance one and qualities many and yet says they are both one and different; she answers that if a quality perishes it perishes for the substance too; and it is said that the reality of the quality is now established.
818.nuance: The verse is a run of quoted speeches each closed by என; who says the last (நன்று...) is not stated, and the reading of line 3 is tentative.
818.event: Ulokan questions Neelakesi's one-and-different thesis and she answers him.

claims.claim: when a quality perishes the substance changes with it

819.reading: Neelakesi explains that seen from the side of the bearer there are no qualities apart, and seen from the side of the qualities the same holds; so one may join or separate them, and with the fourfold reckoning so gained one may decide, and the good of the path is reached.
819.nuance: Lines 1-2 set the two standpoints, of the substance and of the quality, from which the same thing is called one or many; நான்மை (line 3) and துருநெறி (line 4) are not clear, and the fourfold may be the four alternatives of one, different, both and neither.

claims.claim: from the standpoint of the bearer qualities are not separate, and from the standpoint of the quality the same holds

820.reading: The narrator tells how Ulokan, through the method of standpoints, came to the conclusion that the quality has no reality apart from its bearer, that the bearer is one with its quality, and that the qualities are those things themselves, and judged it good.
820.nuance: எய்தினான் (line 4) is masculine: the opponent himself reaches the conclusion, by நயம், the standpoint method. The defeat is recorded as a conversion of judgment, not a rout.
820.event: Ulokan accepts Neelakesi's conclusion by the method of standpoints.

claims.claim: the quality has no reality apart from its bearer, and the bearer is one with its quality

821.reading: Neelakesi bids Ulokan to understand that substance, quality and action have one reality, to make it clear in the threefold path, and to meditate on the red feet of the lord of the path of compassion so that darkness perishes, and so to be.
821.nuance: மும்மை (line 2) is most likely the three jewels of right faith, knowledge and conduct. Darkness ends by the disciple's own understanding and remembering of the lord, not by the lord's act.
821.event: Neelakesi instructs the defeated Ulokan in the Jain path.

claims.claim: substance, quality and action have one reality
meditating on the feet of the compassionate lord dispels darkness

822.reading: Having given Ulokan her parting charge, Neelakesi says she will cross the bamboo-filled forest road, and he answers by asking the sweet-spoken one to think of the pain of parting.
822.nuance: The division of speakers is inferred from the two என்னவே; பேம்படுப்பவரொடும் (line 3) is hard, perhaps parting even from those who once caused fear.
822.event: Neelakesi takes leave of Ulokan, who speaks of the pain of parting.

823.reading: Neelakesi smiles that his words are fitting and true, and tells him that steadily praising the Lord's shrine is the best course; when he says it is right, she leaves.
823.nuance: சேதியம் (line 2) is the caitya, the shrine of the Jina. நக்கனளாகிய may be read as 'she smiled' or as நக்கன் (the unclothed one) with the Lord; the reading takes the first.
823.event: Neelakesi tells Ulokan to worship at the Lord's shrine; he agrees and she departs.

claims.claim: steady praise of the Lord's shrine is the best course

links.note: In 393 Neelakesi told the Buddhist that the quality is the qualified thing and that she holds them both different and one; 804 states the same thesis against the Vaisheshika.
links.teaches: One Jain thesis faces opposite errors: against the Buddhist, who keeps only qualities, she stresses the bearer; against the Vaisheshika, who splits quality from bearer, she stresses their oneness.

links.note: The opening sermon names standpoints (நயன்) among the doors through which the soul and its qualities are examined; 819 and 820 use the standpoints to settle the quality question and win the opponent.
links.teaches: The sermon's list of methods is not decoration: the standpoint it names is the very tool that ends the Vaisheshika debate, by making one and different two views of one thing.

links.note: The sermon promises that in the land of deeds penance drives out dark karma and brings the highest bliss; 807 argues that this needs deeds to be qualities of the soul itself.
links.teaches: The promise of release in the sermon rests on a metaphysics the later debate supplies: only if karma inheres in the soul can penance change the soul and free it.

links.note: Before her first debate Neelakesi bows at the Arhat's shrine; at the end of this one she sends the defeated Ulokan to praise the Lord's shrine.
links.teaches: The debates begin and end in worship at the Jina's shrine, so winning an argument is framed as bringing the loser to the place the debater started from.

links.note: The Manimekalai's Vaisheshika closes his account with inherence joining quality and bearer, and the Buddhist epic lets it stand unanswered; 815 attacks that very relation with a regress.
links.teaches: Read together, the two epics show which Vaisheshika category the rival schools found weakest: the Buddhist work records inherence as the school's last word, the Jain work makes it the first thing to fall.

links.note: The Manimekalai's Vaisheshika makes generality the first common being that lets substance, quality and action work; 813 says the universal is only likeness between things.
links.teaches: What the Vaisheshika in one epic treats as the ground of all working, the Jain in the other reduces to resemblance, so the dispute is over whether the common is a thing or a relation.

links.note: Kural 5 says both kinds of deed, born of darkness, do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's praise; 807 says good and bad deeds and their fruits are qualities of the soul, or birth and release mean nothing.
links.teaches: Both count good deeds with bad as what binds, but the Jain debater asks what clinging is: a deed can cling or fall away only if it is a quality of the soul, which the couplet takes for granted.

gains.a: the verse's technical argument is tied to a plain moral teaching that both good and bad deeds bind
gains.b: the couplet's image of deeds clinging gets a stated account of what the clinging is, which it does not give

links.note: Kural 355 calls understanding the seeing of the true thing in a thing whatever its nature; 819 says thing and quality are one from one standpoint and different from another.
links.teaches: The couplet separates a thing's nature from its truth and asks us to see through to the truth; the Jain standpoint doctrine holds that the separation itself depends on where one looks.

gains.a: the standpoint method is set against a widely held definition of understanding, showing what it adds: a rule for when nature and thing are to be told apart
gains.b: the couplet's split between a thing's nature and its true being is shown to be one possible view, not the only one

links.note: In 821 darkness perishes as the disciple understands the three and remembers the Lord's feet; in Tirumanthiram 2293 the malas leave like evening darkness before a flame by grace.
links.teaches: Both texts end bondage with darkness dispelled, but in the Jain verse the remover is the disciple's own knowledge and remembrance, while the Saiva verse gives the work to grace.

gains.a: the Jain verse's silence about any act of the Lord stands out once set beside a text where the Lord's grace does the work
gains.b: the Saiva image of grace as flame is set against a release with the same image and no giver, which shows grace is its distinctive claim

new_concepts.gloss: a quality borne by a substance (குணி, its bearer); whether the two are one or different is argued between schools
new_concepts.label_source: the verses' own word: குணங்கள் (804), குணம் (818); id as declared in neelakesi ch018

new_concepts.gloss: formal debate between schools, opened by a challenge and held before a king's assembly
new_concepts.label_source: the sarukkam's rubric (வைசேடிக வாதச் சருக்கம்); id as declared in neelakesi ch008

new_concepts.gloss: in Jain teaching a standpoint: a partial view from which a thing is judged one, many, lasting or passing, so that opposed statements hold each in its respect
new_concepts.label_source: the verse's own word: நயத்தில் (820); the sermon's நயன் (120)

source_issues: 811 line 1 reads பாதுவெலா, evidently for பொதுவெலா; line 4's செதுவலாம் is obscure.
810 line 2 reads குழுமிக கெட்டன without the doubled consonant (for குழுமிக் கெட்டன).
814 line 4 reads பொருள ளெண்ணலே with a doubled ள.
819 line 4 துருநெறி and 815 line 4 முனிவு போக்கிதோ are hard to construe and may be corrupt.
823 line 2 நக்கனளாகிய can be divided as நக்கனள் ஆகிய or நக்கன் ஆகிய; the speaker division in 818 and 822 is not marked.
